items.title: Need for Speed Underground 2 online in the browser
items.content:
Post the log in #bug-reports on our Discord , with what you were doing.

The PC game's own code, recompiled for Chrome and Firefox: up to 120 fps in widescreen, free roam and Online races with friends, and controllers, wheels and touch controls.

My brother and I played this game together about 20 years ago. Because of that I tried porting it to the browser so we could play together again. It worked surprisingly well, and it got a bit out of hand. It's great to see so many people playing it.

To help with hosting and development costs, you can buy me a coffee . Everyone gets the same game, with no microtransactions or paid perks. Supporters just get a Discord role.

Help, bugs and questions: our Discord . Rights holders: legal (at) nfsu2.xyz.

Source code on GitHub . Based on Talha Müderrisoğlu's NFSU2Recomp , the original x86 → C static recompiler for NFSU2, after N64: Recompiled and XenonRecomp . This project was forked from NFSU2Recomp's MIT-licensed version of 16 October 2026 and uses only code from that version.

Dubbed voices and movies, and Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Thai text: KyoriAsh's Multi 13 languages mod , with Lee-Ryo's Thai support.

Portuguese (Brazil): TraduMix and MixMods (Fyro, Beater, Kerlyston F.; Junior_Djjr, SideWinder, Elyzandro).

Polish: PLProjekt (Daniel Graszka, MaDeR, Marcin Piech, Nati, Mateusz Wilkowski, alter).

Turkish: Samet Samyeli ; fonts: muntazam .

Czech: ROXOR, PINĎA & syn , with our own edits.

English subtitles: VileStuff's English Subtitles Fixed .

To save while playing: Esc or Start > Garage > Save

Loads your saves and username, and syncs them between your devices.

Changes apply the next time you press Play.

The mods in this game and their makers (translations: the Translations tab). Changes apply the next time you press Play.

Tap the game's menus, or use the arrows, OK and Back beside them. Touch controls show while you drive.

The button at the game's top right switches it too.

Which thumb steers. Moved in keeps the controls off the screen's edges.

With tilt steering, keeps the horizon level.

The game's menu arrows and bottom buttons. Auto makes the arrows finger-sized and leaves the bottom buttons as they are.

In menus: arrow keys and Enter, Esc goes back. Change keys in the game's Options, Controls.

Players with the same crew name always see each other in free roam, in the crew's colour. Type a name to start or join a crew (up to 4).

Join a friend's world: free roam shows its players from now on.

items.title: How are you dealing with all the negative side effects of AI on the web?
items.summary: ask, web
items.content:
It seems to me that the AI hype killed the web for good, but not for the reasons we immediately associate with it.

Search engines now rank links full of slop at the top, which ironically make LLM summaries acceptable, not because they are better than what we had before (they are not), but because they at least mention the good links which are now buried at the bottom of the page. Also, they've been rate limiting ordinary users like crazy: more often than I'd like to, Google and DuckDuckGo now either show me either an error message or tell me to wait a bit. Sometimes I waste at least a minute refreshing the page and waiting for a result.

I also can't browse GitHub freely without being logged in. Anubis is now everywhere, occasionally blocking me. I feel like my productivity has actually gone down thanks to all of that.

Edit: I see that most of the replies here are suggesting relying less on the web and going after more fundamental resources, which are great suggestions, don’t get me wrong! But a book from 5 years ago will not help you understand why your custom firmware doesn’t boot in your 1-year old mobile chipset. A existing bug report on the web probably will. Not quite my predicament at the moment, but something very similar for which the web seemed to work just fine before the AI craze.

I'm still working on Marginalia Search. It's gotten pretty good, but still much to go. Kinda wish more people saw this all as a fun and interesting engineering problem rather than just moping about it.

I think AI gets a lot of blame for a state of disrepair that was already quite present even before AI came around. It's exacerbated a lot of the existing problems and added a few new ones, but even in 2021-2023 the web was a monumental shit hole with barely functioning search and discovery capabilities. Astroturfing pre clawd-era was a bit more limited as you had to be a state actor or employ rooms full of people in low income countries to do it, but let's not pretend it wasn't already a big problem.

It's more of a dark forest now than it was back then, in a combination of increased bot activity and the dead sea effect of people who give a fuck about quality conversation being the most sensitive to decline in quality and leaving first. Finding actual high quality human interaction on the web has never been harder.

I think that's the biggest unsolved problem we're facing now. All the solutions for solving the bot problem seem to revolve around dystopian slippery slope tech like device attestation and tying digital identity to physical identity. Not at all happy with that one.

Thank you! For Marginalia (exactly the kind of walk-the-walk we need), and for avoiding defeatism.

Finding actual high quality human interaction on the web has never been harder.

Indeed. It's gotten harder and harder over the years; big tech and social media ruined so much of it.

And yet I interact with humans online all day most days. Here for one example

Yes, I don't think I or the comment OP were saying otherwise, only that it's harder to have "actual high quality human interaction on the web".

As I moved to classic forums, IRC and Mastodon my interactions with humans peaked again. Nobody is trying to sell me something.

Yeah the attestation and identity mechanisms, enforced by state legislation, point to the end state (predicted by net neutrality activists)[https://www.lukekehoe.com/wesupportnetneutrality.html]: internet access akin to cable tv: you pay $N for facebook+netflix, $M for facebook+netflix+youtube, etc, etc. Plus, what you can see and read is highly regulated and monitored.

Personally, I think the small web will need to somehow fork itself off of the mainstream www. I don't know how that will happen, and whether overlay networks will play a role, but we're looking at a speciation process for websites.

items.title_ko: AI가 웹에 미친 부작용, 여러분은 어떻게 대응하고 계신가요?
items.summary_ko: 글쓴이는 AI 열풍이 웹을 되돌릴 수 없을 만큼 망가뜨렸다고 주장한다. 검색 결과 상단에 저품질 링크가 올라오고, Google과 DuckDuckGo는 일반 사용자의 검색을 자주 제한하며, GitHub은 로그인 없이 보기 어렵고 Anubis가 자주 접속을 막는다고 설명한다. 그 결과 생산성이 떨어졌다고 토로한다.
items.content_ko: 글쓴이는 AI 열풍이 웹을 망쳤지만 흔히 떠올리는 이유와는 다른 이유 때문이라고 말한다. 검색엔진은 저품질 링크를 상단에 올리고, 그 탓에 LLM 요약이 오히려 받아들여진다. 요약이 나은 결과라서가 아니라, 좋은 링크를 언급해 주기 때문이라는 것이다. 또한 Google과 DuckDuckGo가 일반 사용자의 요청을 심하게 제한해 오류 메시지가 뜨거나 잠시 기다리라는 안내가 나오고, 결과를 보려고 1분 넘게 새로고침하는 일도 있다고 한다. GitHub은 로그인 없이 자유롭게 둘러보기 어렵고, Anubis가 곳곳에 있어 가끔 접속을 막는다. 댓글에서는 웹 대신 기초 자료에 더 의존하라는 제안이 많았다. 글쓴이는 이 제안에 동의하면서도, 5년 전 책으로는 최신 모바일 칩셋에서 커스텀 펌웨어가 부팅되지 않는 이유를 알기 어렵고, 기존 버그 리포트가 웹에 있으면 도움이 된다고 반박한다.

items.title: Developer ends lucrative screensaver deal with Roku because Fox bought it
items.content:
Some Roku OS users have been sad to learn that their favorite screensaver will no longer be available as of December 1.

This week, affected users reported receiving an alert on their device that they will not be able to use the “Aquatic Life” screensaver after this month, as first reported by Cord Cutters News .

The screensaver has been an option for Roku OS users for 10 years. Roku has been licensing the animation, which is called the Marine Aquarium , from artist Jim Sachs through Prolific Publishing.

Sachs is the creator and copyright holder of the Marine Aquarium. He developed the screensaver through his company SereneScreen . He tells Ars Technica that the licensing agreement with Roku is up for renewal every October and can be canceled by either party for any reason. A day after learning that Fox was planning to buy Roku , a deal that closed today , Sachs told Prolific that he wouldn’t be renewing Roku’s license.

“I can’t be part of the Fox world,” he tells Ars, pointing to Fox News’ controversial style of news and entertainment.

Roku will automatically switch the Aquatic Life screensaver on affected devices to the Roku City screensaver, another popular animation that includes subtle advertisements , according to the user notice.

The Aquatic Life screensaver provided an ad-free, relaxing display for years for some Roku users. Numerous people online have lamented the impending loss of the screensaver for Roku OS .

“When my head is in overdrive (very often with my ADHD), this screensaver grounds me and lets me exhale and become focused with myself again. It may sound over the top, but it’s true. It takes a lot for me to chill and relax, but this Aquatic Life [screensaver] is my go to. Totally gutted 😢,” a Reddit user wrote this week.

Sachs told Ars he’s interested in placating fans of the Marine Aquarium and said Roku has asked him to restore the license. When asked what his biggest concerns about Fox buying Roku are, Sachs said:

It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can’t stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole.

The decision to not renew the licensing contract has “major financial consequences,” Sachs said.

“Our needs are very small, with a high property tax bill being the only significant expense,” he said. “We’ll be okay but can’t start any of the projects I had planned.”

According to Sachs, the licensing “agreement was $80,000 per year for exclusive rights to all set-top devices, or $60,000 per year for non-exclusive. They have always opted for exclusive.” Ars asked Roku to confirm the details of the licensing agreement but didn’t hear back ahead of publication.

The licensing deal with Roku was Sachs’ primary form of income, he told Ars, noting low sales of the version of the screensaver for computers.

Marine Aquarium fans can still buy the screensaver for Windows, macOS, iOS, and Android, but it seems unlikely that it will return to the Roku platform.

“One of the best reasons to buy Roku was the themes and less ads than competitors. But they haven’t added any new themes in years aside from sponsored ones, and they increased the amount of ads,” a Reddit user posted this week in response to Roku’s loss of the Aquatic Life screensaver.

Sachs, meanwhile, says he has “no delusions” that pulling the license will have any meaningful impact. However, he’s hopeful that another streaming company will look to offer the screensaver.

“I’m assuming that Fox will not be reversing their whole rage-based business model and take responsibility for all the harm it has caused. I’d be happy to restore the license under those circumstances. They could even have it for free,” he said.

Fox closed its acquisition of Roku today for $22 billion.

items.title: What a site can read about you without a permission prompt: notes from building a 118-signal self-check page
items.content:
The checks run in your browser. This site's servers answer three kinds of request only: /api/me (what they see in this very request anyway: your address, Cloudflare's data on it and the headers), /api/etag (a random ID that shows how the browser cache recognizes you, not kept by the server) and the anonymous counts below. The site's own probe, probe.1ms.dog, looks at this connection itself (the TCP packets, the TLS handshake, the start of HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) to tell your system and whether something sits in between. None of them keeps a log.

To tell you how common your values are, the page then adds one to anonymous counters: how many checks had this system, browser, screen, graphics card, time zone and first language, the first 8 characters of each fingerprint ID, how each check came out that day, and how long each run took (a range such as 3–5 seconds; a run not done 45 seconds in counts once as stuck). There's no IP, no full fingerprint and no record of a single visit, just one number per value. "Don't count me" under the fingerprint card turns this off for this browser. A browser that sends Global Privacy Control is never counted.

To find your exits and your DNS resolver, the page also contacts a few outside services directly (named in the right column: IPIP.NET, IP.SB, the Cloudflare trace on chatgpt.com, claude.ai and cloudflare.com, Cloudflare Radar, ip-api's DNS server, and two STUN servers). They see your address, as any site you visit does. Everything else is read in your browser and stays there. The code is open source.

Your last visit is remembered only in your own browser's storage and never sent anywhere (it's separate from the anonymous counts): the time, fingerprint and city of that visit, so the page can show whether it recognized you. The × on the ID card deletes it. A shared link carries the portrait without your address or city. The "Stored traces" row also writes one random tag into localStorage, IndexedDB, Cache Storage and window.name, again only in your browser, to show whether clearing one store is enough; the × deletes those too. Tracker blocking, precise location and motion sensors run only when you press their button: the tracker test asks 7 tracking companies for their scripts, and they see your address; the location and sensor readings are worked out in the page, never sent.
items.title_ko: 권한 요청 없이 웹사이트가 알 수 있는 정보: 118개 신호 자가진단 페이지 제작기
items.summary_ko: 이 자가진단 페이지의 검사는 브라우저에서 실행된다. 서버는 요청 정보, 브라우저 캐시 식별용 임의 ID, 익명 집계값만 받으며, 사이트 측은 어떤 것도 로그로 남기지 않는다고 설명한다. 집계에는 IP나 전체 지문, 개별 방문 기록이 포함되지 않고 값별 횟수만 더해진다.
items.content_ko: 검사는 사용자의 브라우저에서 실행된다. 사이트 서버는 세 가지 요청에만 응답한다. /api/me는 이 요청에 이미 포함된 IP 주소, Cloudflare가 제공하는 관련 데이터, 헤더 정보를 돌려준다. /api/etag는 브라우저 캐시가 사용자를 어떻게 인식하는지 보여 주는 임의 ID이며 서버에 저장되지 않는다. 익명 집계도 있다. 사이트의 탐침 probe.1ms.dog는 TCP 패킷, TLS 핸드셰이크, HTTP/2와 HTTP/3 연결 초기 단계를 살펴보아 시스템과 중간 장치 존재 여부를 알아낸다. 사이트 측은 어떤 것도 로그를 남기지 않는다고 설명한다. 값이 얼마나 흔한지 알려주기 위해 페이지는 익명 카운터에 값을 더한다. 집계 항목은 시스템, 브라우저, 화면, 그래픽카드, 시간대, 첫 번째 언어, 지문 ID 앞 8자, 검사 결과, 실행 시간(3~5초 같은 범위)이다. 45초가 지나도 끝나지 않은 실행은 'stuck'으로 한 번 집계된다. IP, 전체 지문, 개별 방문 기록은 없고 값마다 숫자 하나만 더해진다. 지문 카드 아래의 'Don't count me'를 누르면 해당 브라우저의 집계가 꺼지며, Global Privacy Control 신호를 보내는 브라우저는 집계에서 제외된다.

items.title: 사생활침해, 개인정보보호법 위반, 명예훼손, 사이버불링 정황 공론화
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

items.title: Every Mac comes with an (undocumented) family member classifier
items.content:
Every Mac since macOS 13 (2022) ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, what you do and when. In this post, we look into how this system works and give you a tool to peek into your own graph.

A family fork: one knight on e2 attacks White's king, queen, rook and bishop at once. White's pieces are the household the graph is about; the knight is the store, one move from every one of them. White's own last move, 18.e3 , emptied the square it stands on. White is in check and has one legal reply, Kh1 ; then the knight takes the queen. The check falls on the one who accepted the terms. What is lost is someone else.

3r1rk1/pp2qppp/8/3p1b2/8/1NQ1P1B1/PP2nPPP/2R2RK1 w - - 1 19

What if I told you that every Mac since 2022 ships a pair of daemons whose only purpose in life is to build a graph about you and the people around you: who you are, who you know, how those people are related to you and to each other, how you communicate with them, where you go, with whom, what you do and when. This graph is built on device by cross-referencing pretty much everything on the machine: Contacts, Calendar, Photos, Messages, Mail, location, Screen Time and a long tail of behavioral signals. And, more importantly, it is held as a queryable store that LLMs retrieve from (allegedly). Would you believe me?

Well, that's what is happening, and interestingly enough, there is little documentation of how this whole mechanism works on your Mac. The closest thing to an official description is the man page ( man 8 knowledgeconstructiond ), and this is all you get:

Previous work: To be fair, Apple's own researchers did publish a paper on the techniques behind this graph construction, back in 2023. But there is next to nothing on how it is integrated into macOS: which versions run it, and the exact list of what is collected and inferred. And not a word about the "kinship" inference discussed below. Also, we personally ran into it while doing some security research on the Apple Intelligence bundle in macOS 26 in August 2026; but a few months before, Nic Lydon came across the same database and wrote it up in I Built a Personal Knowledge Graph. Apple Had Already Built One on My Laptop. And even more recently, a forensics tool went looking on the phone: in September 2026, Alexis Brignoni taught iLEAPP to read the same store on iOS, where graph.db and the ontology.db that decodes its predicate codes sit under /private/var/mobile/Library/IntelligencePlatform ; he writes it up in Reading the iPhone Knowledge Graph, and Checking Its Work .

This blog post is an account of some analysis work we carried out on what the knowledge graph actually does, so that you (the user) can get a better understanding of how this mechanism works, and some clarity on what the graph holds about you and your family and friends. Everything in it was collected on macOS 26 (26.6.2 at the time of writing).

To this end, we open-source a local dashboard ( iKnow ) you can use to read the content of your personal knowledge graph on your Mac.

Finally, we derail a bit and look into what we do best: weaponizing and exploiting. We run a thought experiment (one that applies to any such personalized system) and show what happens if such a knowledge base ends up in the wrong hands, and how a "privacy single point of failure" can be exploited to threaten you in ways you may not have considered before (when combined with an abliterated LLM).

The two daemons keep their work in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform , a directory of SQLite databases (fifty-one databases) stored in plaintext but located in a zone protected by TCC Full Disk Access.

Likely, the most interesting is graph.db . It is a triple store written in a vocabulary of 181 entity classes and 278 predicates: every row is a subject, a predicate and an object. The subject is an entity…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?
items.content:
Hot fridges, a fake nuclear alert and a $6bn heist: are we in the foothills of a hacking epidemic?

As AI exposes flaws in IT systems and geopolitics plays out on the cyber frontline, some experts say the events of recent weeks could soon be a common occurence

Alex Pearce was doing the morning rounds at his fruit and vegetable wholesale business in London on Monday last week when he noticed something odd.

The defrost light on refrigeration unit 2 was on, and the panel reading was 150C. Unit 4 was the same.

As he approached his biggest unit, its defrost light also blinked on.

It was at this point that Pearce thought: is this a cyber-attack? He walked over to the box connecting the units to the internet and yanked out the cable.

Alex Pearce unplugged the internet at his wholesale fruit and vegetable business after seeing the temperature of the refrigeration units shoot up. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian On the same day, retailers in Belgium , Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported similar problems, with refrigerators and freezers in some shops soaring to as high as 50C (122F).

“If it had happened on a Saturday morning, when I don’t tend to be here, it could ultimately have led to a fire,” Pearce said.

But it is not just Pearce and a disparate group of retailers, as well as French blood banks , that have been suffering.

The hacking attack was one of three over a number of days. On 30 October, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, was robbed of $6.3bn (£4.7bn) in a record heist and on 1 November hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app, sending people in Kyiv a fake nuclear strike alert .

Hackers targeted Ukraine’s emergency alert app this month to send warnings to people in Kyiv. Photograph: Roman Pilipey/AFP/Getty Images The official message after the fridge attacks is: expect more disruption. We are in the “foothills” of a new hacking landscape, the head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre said this week.

Referring to flaws in IT systems that are being exposed by AI technology, the NCSC boss, Richard Horne, said: “There are so many vulnerabilities out there that … you could say are waiting to be exploited.”

He added: “The most serious risk we face in the short term is just a huge rise in the volume of incidents … and I think you could probably point to the last few months and say we’ve started to see that.”

Websites around the world were temporarily taken out of service as a precaution last month when AI technology from the ChatGPT developer OpenAI helped discover a flaw in PHP , a computer language used to build much of the world wide web. French supermarket fridges were also attacked last month in what could have been a trial run for the more expansive foray this week .

Boxes of perished goods outside an Intermarché in Paris last month after a cyber-attack that could have been a trial run for this week’s foray. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters To Azeem Azhar, a tech entrepreneur and commentator, the way AI models were discovering flaws that assailants could harness recalled China’s Covid ground zero. This was, he said, a “ Wuhan moment ”.

Azar’s assertion headlined a Substack post that also quoted the cybersecurity executive Matthew Prince, who said last month: “We’re going to have a couple of years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

items.title: What I run on my $10 USD OpenStick homelab
items.content:
A while ago I bought an OpenStick on a whim for 10 dollars (including shipping!) because it seemed like such a cool novelty piece of hardware.

Now, you might look at this hardware and think “my watch is more powerful than that”, and you wouldn’t necessarily be wrong, but there’s still a lot of fun to be had with a device this size, and it’s a great gadget to get started with self-hosting.

The installation process is a bit involved, but once you’re up and running it runs Debian, which brings all the classic goodies such as systemd (among other things, a scheduler and service monitoring for Linux) and Podman (lightweight containerization). For 10 USD you basically get a home server with minimal power usage and zero noise!

There’s actually a lot of useful software that runs great on this thing. Some of my favorites are:

This is a little service that connects to any running Google Cast device and skips sponsorships (and sometimes ads). It barely uses any resources, and after a while you forget that it exists, but it does make the whole YouTube experience a lot nicer!

AdGuard Home blocks bad domains at the DNS level: spyware, malware, and so on. These days devices have a tendency to spy on you. Smart TVs run content recognition continuously, washing machines scan your network, and your coffee maker might be spying on you.

A DNS blocker cannot block all bad requests (you’ll need a proper firewall for that), but it sure can block a whole lot. After adding a few blocklists, 60% of my queries are now blocked. Most seem harmless, but I’m pretty sure that some aren’t.

I’m running my own fork, which can handle large blocklists in an efficient manner, but you probably shouldn’t run binaries provided by random strangers, so I’ve also included the link to the official version below (which is totally fine if you limit yourself to smaller blocklists).

AdGuard Home Next-Gen - 40 MB (independent of the size of the blocklist)

AdGuard Home - 40 MB (with a small (200k) blocklist)

Zeroclaw is an AI agent harness. It supports 30 channels (Telegram, email, WhatsApp, etc.), has sensible security defaults, a nice web UI, and integrations with all the major LLM providers.

I ran OpenClaw for a while on my Kubernetes cluster, but it mostly caused a lot of frustration: it worked, but it used 1 GB+ of memory, broke with every update, and they kept changing functionality in ways that broke my existing workflows. Zeroclaw feels like a breath of fresh air. It uses ~3 MB RSS when idle, covers all the functionality that I need, and the security defaults are sensible and easy enough to disable. The next version will (hopefully!) have rich message support for Telegram, implemented by yours truly. The PR can be tracked here!

I’ve given Zeroclaw access to the OpenStick (but nothing beyond that). Effectively it’s a root shell, but given that the blast radius is limited, I figured it would be acceptable. I mostly use this to monitor the OpenStick, with questions such as “anything in the logs that requires my attention?” or “how is the disk space?”. The biggest advantage is that it communicates through Telegram, so if I’m in the mountains with limited signal, I can still ask it how my little server is doing :)

I looked at alternatives such as Picoclaw and Nullclaw, and no doubt they’re good as well. However, Zeroclaw seemed to have the best documentation and the most active community, so I went with that :)

Cloudflared makes it possible to expose all these services securely to the big, bad internet, for free, without exposing any ports. The downside might be that the NSA might be able to read everything you do, but for a homelab I consider that to be an acceptable trade-off.

Beszel shows a pretty graph of memory, CPU usage, and so on, and alerts you if something looks suspicious, all while using very little memory.

I ran Grafana and the whole stack on my Kubernetes cluster for a while, and it’s powerful, but not extremely user friendly, and it felt like…

items.title: I’m not a fan of Deno’s security model (2024)
items.summary: security
items.content:
this has been bothering me for a while now, so I want to write down my thoughts

so I can get it out of my head and move on. we’re gonna talk about how Deno approaches

security, specifically with its permissions system, and why I think this approach

is fundamentally insecure and misleading.

Deno is a language runtime for JavaScript. it consists of a standard library, a package manager,

a TypeScript transpiler and a bunch of other stuff that’s not important for our story. it’s not

a JavaScript implementation , so it does not interpret or compile JavaScript, it reuses V8 for that.

one of the flagship features of Deno is its permission system

(it’s under the “Secure by default” header on their landing page ).

the idea is simple: as JS code running in Deno needs the standard library to access the outside world,

Deno can choose which accesses it allows or disallows, so when you run

the standard library will only allow code.ts to read /tmp/dir and run uname .

additionally, a program can request permissions at runtime, so code like

will display a nice little prompt in the terminal:

(aside: I really miss this feature in browser extensions. currently, if your extension needs potential

access to any website, it needs to request actual access to all the websites, which is less than ideal)

if you like puzzles, this is the point where you can stop and think about what could go wrong with this system.

of the two specific issues I want to point out this is the less severe one.

we’ll discuss it first because this was the first thing I noticed and it kinda immediately irked me when I first read

(if you’re only interested in the more juicy part, you can skip to the next section ).

so, this nice little prompt is displayed in the terminal. it’s not, like, a PolKit GUI window or anything,

it’s just text on stdout waiting for input from stdin. this is a wild thing to do.

you see, terminal has a somewhat weird API. most of the commands / requests application can send to the terminal

are sent in-band, by printing them to stdout. terminal can then reply by sending data to stdin.

as Deno allows programs to print arbitrary data to stdout and read from stdin without requiring any permissions

or doing any filtering, malicious code can send arbitrary commands to the terminal. it’s usually okay,

because terminals won’t, like, execute shell commands just because stdout told them to, you’re supposed

to be able to freely cat files without risking arbitrary code execution. it’s markedly less okay if

you allow malicious code to do whatever with the terminal and then print a prompt on the same exact terminal.

you could, like, hide the prompt by messing with terminal colors .

(this one got closed in 2026 because the permission prompt is “partially visible”

(you can see an emoji) and “AI agents tend to” change terminal colors, so that’s a “valid use-case”)

or trick the user into pre-feeding approval into stdin .

or trick the terminal into feeding approval into stdin as a response to some request .

(terminal won’t ever send Enter to stdin to avoid executing commands, but “press Enter to continue”

is common enough to not be suspicious; the user never sees the actual prompt).

the specific issue on the screencast is long patched; the issue with terminal colors is not.

that doesn’t really matter because the real issue is using an attacker-controlled channel for

security-sensitive information. it’s like executing attacker-controlled JS code on a webpage

and then asking for password on the same page. you can’t know that the page is in a safe state,

even if Deno manages to patch every single issue with the “standard” escape codes, you never know

which non-standard codes even exist out there. many terminals have some, it’s impossible to predict

how they will interact with your prompt.

(aside: how come sudo can do it then? the difference is that sudo asks for the password first,

before running any other code. to trick sudo that way…

A ‘customer success story’: leaked documents show Cisco doubled down on Israeli military deals during Gaza war

Tech giant leaped to shore up relationship even as company was roiled by worker protest over its role in the war

A year into the war in Gaza , the networks of Israel ’s military intelligence community were plagued with technical problems. There were major, multi-hour outages to their systems, and repeated crashes. Built-in debugging mechanisms failed.

The problems, which started as intelligence operations were undergoing updates to digital infrastructure, became so persistent as to undermine the “confidence” of Israeli intelligence agencies in one of their top network providers: the multinational tech conglomerate Cisco .

“This series of events happened during the period of war, deeply impacting customer sentiment,” warned a confidential memo drafted by Cisco and obtained by the Guardian. “During a period of national conflict, these repeated outages severely impacted critical operations.”

The September 2025 draft memo was part of a trove of internal documents leaked by Cisco workers furious with the company’s ties to Israel’s military three years into the war, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians.

Cisco, one of the largest tech companies in the world and at one point the single most valuable , is often described as selling the “plumbing” of the internet. It provides the routers, servers and communications systems that move data for companies, governments and militaries around the globe. While its business ties to the Israeli military have received less scrutiny than those of other tech giants, the company has worked with the Israeli security state for years. Israel’s military intelligence contracts alone generated about $67m in business in three years, according to a 2025 document reviewed by the Guardian.

Revealed: Israel demanded Google and Amazon use secret ‘wink’ to sidestep legal orders

While Cisco’s involvement with Israel’s military before and since 2023 has been documented before, the leaked documents obtained by the Guardian reveal the lengths the company went to in order to preserve and expand the relationship as the war in Gaza dragged on. They also show that earlier this year, Splunk – a Cisco subsidiary platform that can process and analyze massive volumes of machine-generated data – made a pitch to join the controversial cloud computing contract between the Israeli government, Google and Amazon known as Project Nimbus .

Cisco pursued these opportunities as the mass killing of civilians in Gaza was amply documented, international organizations and governments began to refer to Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide, and the company itself was roiled by internal turmoil over its own role in the war.

Cisco did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Israeli military wrote in a statement to the Guardian: “The [Israel Defense Forces] is assisted by services provided by a range of companies to meet its ongoing needs and objectives. The IDF does not intend to comment on matters relating to contracts or services provided by other entities.”

Members of Bridge to Humanity , a group of current and former Cisco workers who have objected to the company’s role in the Gaza war, called the company’s work with Israeli intelligence a “shocking and complete contradiction of values Cisco sells to us employees and externally to its customers, investors, and the public”. They said the company, which pitches itself internally and to the public as an ethics-driven company , had become “an instrument of genocide”.

items.title: Apple’s grey list: Words and phrases your iPhone won’t help you spell
items.content:
The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

The swipe-type-thwarting list was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman. Photograph: Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters

Struggling to spell ‘male chauvinist pig’? Apple’s grey list means your iPhone won’t help you

There are more than 100,000 words and phrases that the tech giant has restricted its predictive text from completing, research shows

“Australia is a very bad place to question your sexuality on MDMA with NSA spies” might be a text you would wish to send to your friends, if you have had an extraordinarily complicated night out in Sydney.

But your iPhone won’t help you spell any of it if you try to swipe-type it – that is, by gliding a finger across a keyboard as opposed to pecking out a word.

New research shows that Apple has a “grey list” of more than 100,000 words and phrases that it has restricted from being completed by its predictive text.

So if a user wishes to type phrases such as “Dictator Trump”, “NSA spies” or, surprisingly, “Australia is a very bad place”, “question your sexuality” or “on MDMA”, they will have to spell them out.

Apple’s predictive text will not suggest these words. And, if a user attempts to swipe-type them, they will often stumble, changing “United Ireland” to “United Iceland”, for example, or “Tibetan independence” to “Tibetan independences”.

The “grey list” was discovered by the independent researcher Derik Kauffman, whose other projects include using AI to find errors in scientific papers. After noticing that he had problems typing certain phrases – but not others – on his iPhone, Kauffman was able to unearth a table containing the list, encoded in Apple’s operating system.

The list he found includes some unsurprising words and phrases. Apple’s iPhone will not autocomplete references to drugs, sexual acts and, perhaps in the spirit of corporate protection, “iMessage isn’t working”.

But it also includes possibly politically charged phrases, which Kauffman described to Reuters as a “light-touch form of censorship”. Among these are “Trayvon Martin”, the name of the Black teenager shot in Florida in 2012, “Kashmir dispute”, “Muslim extremist” and “male chauvinist pig”.

In Hebrew, Apple will not autocomplete the phrase “the occupied territories”. In Arabic, it will not autocomplete the phrase “the Hamas movement”.

The list is one more glimpse into the dark bowels of how autocorrect – the chirpy keyboard partner that helps you look more educated to your loved ones – actually works.

The technology has taken many forms. In its earliest version, Unix, an operating system, would look up each word a user typed against a table of words, to determine if this word was spelled correctly.

Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices

This evolved into n-grams, a tool which allows an operating system to statistically predict what words might come next, based on the words before it. These form the basis of Apple’s familiar autocorrect , which was known to change expletives into prudish alternatives: “fork” and “ducking”, among other gaffes.

Last year, Apple launched a new autocorrect – a “transformer-based” system that was more akin to an LLM. Reddit sleuths saw this as a possible reason behind a spate of avant-garde spelling suggestions their iPhones made last year.

This hard-coded list illuminates one longstanding mystery behind the world’s spelling coach. Others remain, such as a brief glitch in which users of the dictation feature saw the name “Trump” flash across their screen when they spoke the word “racist” into their iPhones – which Apple quickly remedied.

Apple said that it designed its keyboard to avoid offering inappropriate or offensive predictive suggestions. It said iPhone users could always type out specific words or phrases, and override predictive text suggestions to achieve their desired meaning.

items.title: Dear Open Source Developers: It's OK not to embargo
items.summary: security
items.content:
Something really important just happened with vulnerability disclosure and open source. No, it’s not PHP and that dumpster fire of a week.

I speak of something Curl just did that probably won’t make the news anywhere because to most people it won’t really make sense. Curl just announced that all low and medium security reports should go into the public issue tracker instead of being privately reported

The basic idea is for vulnerabilities rated low and medium severity, they will be treated like regular old bugs instead of a special bug that needs extra attention. I think this is a great idea and a policy we should be encouraging open source projects to adopt something similar. Open source projects are drowning in vulnerability reports, this should help remove some of the pressure.

In the world of security vulnerabilities, there’s this idea we call an embargo. If someone finds a security vulnerability in something, open source, closed source, it doesn’t matter what. You report this to the vendor/project in private and give them some time to fix the vulnerability. This makes sense for security bugs, the intention being there is time to get the fix ready before it goes public and the attackers start popping shells.

We do this for pretty much all vulnerabilities. Even the really boring ones. Every project, every vendor, everything. It’s just the way it’s always been done, so we keep doing it. This made sense when there were a few hundred vulnerabilities reported per year. We now have a few hundred CVEs being reported per day. It’s not 2005 anymore, we need to stop pretending it is.

Your first thought might be “isn’t a private report better?” and this is where things enter the truth is stranger than fiction part of the story.

You know how when you go to a presentation and the presenter will ask a question that has 3 answers on the screen and the correct answer is always the most unlikely one? That’s basically what’s happening here.

It seems like privately reporting all security bugs is a good thing. It gives projects time to understand the bug, and create a fix, then release the fix all before the bad guys know what’s happening. Everyone wins!

Except that’s not what really happens. Dealing with security embargoes in private is really hard to do. You have to be mindful of who you tell, you have to remember who knows what details about which bug as you probably have more than one thing in flight at a time. You can’t use the public git repos because that will leak the fix. That also means no CI testing. You can’t ask for a review from a community reviewer, or community testing because it’s a secret fix. Maybe the emails are encrypted, so you have to remember your PGP password and where you keep the key. You get the idea. The usual process falls apart, it’s mentally exhausting for anyone doing this. There’s a reason big companies have teams dedicated to doing this sort of work and only this (and even then they screw it up all the time).

When most embargoes leak it’s not because someone is dumb, it leaks because someone forgot a step in this 300 step process.

Now do this for free, and do it 100 times a month. That’s open source today. Every. Single. Project.

Open source is getting hammered with security vulnerabilities #

One other important bit of backstory we need to cover is that every single software manufacturer is getting slammed with vulnerability reports. All of them. Open source developers are seeing large increases in the vulnerability reports they are getting. Closed source vendors are releasing more security fixes in a month now than they used to release in a year.

Also keep in mind that in open source these are volunteers. A lot of them aren’t being paid to work on their projects. They spend nights and weekends working on this stuff. They started out wanting to build a fun simple library to make memes, and now they only handle vulnerability reports.

It used to be really hard to find security vulnerabilities…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub
items.content:
Passwords and API keys that developers typed into commands they approved in Claude Code are sitting in public GitHub repositories, where anyone can read them.

When a user selects " Yes, and don't ask again ," Anthropic's AI coding assistant can save the command, word-for-word, including the secret, in a project settings file.

Software security company Apiiro said yesterday that 1,122 public copies of that file hold at least one secret, though it did not test whether any still work. One company the researchers notified earlier this week confirmed its key had been live.

The file is .claude/settings.local.json. Removing it from a project does not undo the leak, because older versions stay in git history and in forks of the repository. The researchers' advice is to rotate first: change every password, token, and key the file has ever held, then clean up.

By default, Claude Code asks before it runs most shell commands. If the user picks "Yes, and don't ask again," it saves an allow rule in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project, according to its permissions documentation . Matching commands then run without asking in later sessions.

The rule covers only what the prompt offered. Sometimes that is a pattern, such as npm test *, and sometimes one exact command. When it is the exact command, any password or token typed into it is saved too, in plain text.

In public files, the researchers found saved commands with the secret still inside, and they reproduced the behavior with the latest models, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Claude Code tries to keep the file out of git. The first time it writes the file in a git repository, it adds the file to the user's global git excludes, its settings documentation says. Git on that computer then ignores the file in every repository.

That protection stays in one user's git settings on one computer. It does nothing for a file that was already committed, the researchers say. Claude Code never adds the file to the project's own .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the project.

In 539 of the 1,105 repositories the researchers traced, a commit listing Claude as a co-author changed the file. They take this to mean Claude often commits the file itself.

Apiiro's search of public GitHub found 104,185 copies of the file in 103,617 repositories, its research write-up shows. About 1.1% of them, or 1,122 copies, hold at least one secret. Together they hold 1,379 different secrets.

A value counted as a secret when it matched a known key format, or when a password or token sat beside the address of a public server. An AI reviewer also had to agree. The researchers do not say whether anyone has used these secrets.

More than a third of the secrets open a database directly, including 379 database passwords. Others include 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 tokens for GitHub, GitLab and npm, and 23 AWS keys.

Among the owners of these files are 63 organizations, mostly software companies of all sizes. The strongest cases include a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key and the owner password of a medical-records database, the researchers say.

As of Monday, every file with a secret was still on its repository's default branch, and in half of those repositories it had been there for at least 217 days.

Older versions of the file contain 734 more secrets across 509 repositories that are not present in any current copy, usually because the file was deleted. Forks spread the files further: 211 forks of 74 repositories carry the same secrets as the originals.

Secrets also sit in 298 of 76,011 copies of the shared .claude/settings.json file, which teams commit on purpose, mostly inside allow rules. Including those, the older versions, and saved agent chat logs, the total is 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories.

Of 16 coding agents whose documentation the researchers compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save the full approved command in a project file by default.

One small program does it all: it downloads the latest MeccanicOS, checks it,

and makes a USB drive (16 GB or larger) bootable with Ventoy , with MeccanicOS on it.

(On macOS, where Ventoy does not run, it writes MeccanicOS directly to the drive.)

Double-click it and allow it to make changes. If Windows warns about an unknown publisher: More info → Run anyway .

In Terminal (Apple silicon; on an Intel Mac use mos-usb-macos-x86_64 ):

In a terminal (on ARM use mos-usb-linux-arm64 ):

Every MeccanicOS USB drive has a MeccanicOS-README.pdf on it: how to start the computer from the drive, and the BIOS settings if it does not.

Stuck, or have a question? Ask in the MeccanicOS group .

Built on NixOS, but designed as one coherent system instead of a collection of unrelated Linux tools.

No start menu. Super+Space opens one command bar for apps, commands, websites, folders and questions.

The desktop, the included apps and the drivers are on the stick, and installing needs no network. More apps and local AI models are downloaded once, when you ask for them.

Installed: the whole disk encrypted (LUKS2). Live: the session stays in memory, and your vaults and persistent home are encrypted. A hardened kernel, a firewall, login alerts. For convenience sudo asks no password, and an installed system has an SSH server (keys only) that is off until you turn it on.

One way to open any file, one look for every tool, apps named by what they do: "Web Browser (Brave)".

The whole system is one Nix flake. Upgrades are atomic: a failed one changes nothing, and you can roll back.

MeccanicOS comes with a large collection of drivers and firmware (all of it freely redistributable): Mesa and Vulkan, video acceleration, PipeWire, Bluetooth, printers and scanners, NVIDIA's driver picked by itself. Hardening never gets in a driver's way.

Only freely redistributable software, so you may share any ISO you build.

Type part of an app name, a website, a command, a path ( ~/Documents opens it in yazi) or !command to run it in a new shell. ?question asks the AI.

Run from USB with nothing kept, keep your home encrypted on the stick, or install to the disk from one page. What survives a restart .

LUKS2 vaults in the stick's free space, and on Ventoy sticks as files next to the ISO.

open FILE works like on a Mac, and the same rules apply in the shell, yazi, mc, fzf and on a double-click.

Local AI after a one-time model download (Qwen3 through Ollama, ~2.5 GB; then offline, and nothing leaves the computer), or Claude, ChatGPT or Grok with your API key (your questions go to that company).

Copy any text and an offline voice (Piper) reads it, sentence by sentence.

An alert on an SSH login from somewhere new or an SSH attack, never more than a few an hour. One key disconnects everything.

Encrypted, every night or when you plug in the disk, or to the cloud. Get back any earlier version of a file from a right-click.

Common settings in one place, exported to another computer in one file; a doctor that finds problems and offers a fix.

Text grows with large and sharp screens by itself; icons keep their size.

VictorMono Nerd Font, Atuin history, fzf, zoxide, yazi with image previews and drag and drop.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

items.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group
items.content:
In 2023 after the ChatGPT release, it was clear to me that research needed to be more organized to succeed than was typical within Microsoft Research . The amount of support and focus which other research groups were applying was great enough that even with a clever idea pursued by one person it was likely to arrive late and unconvincing because one person could not move fast enough and the baselines which one person could assemble just were not strong enough to really show that an idea was worth taking flight. Several other folks thought similarly and we organized to create the AI Frontiers sub-organization within MSR.

In AI Frontiers, we actively tried to organize coherent research efforts. This was not precisely “top down” or “bottom up”, but rather mostly somewhere in the messy middle. There were disagreements of course, and resolving them was sometimes quite challenging. Compute availability was also an often-severe bottleneck. But at a high level I was under the general impression that the organization was succeeding in doing pioneering things, particularly given the small size of AIF (~50 people) and relative to what we could do previously. Much of the work of AIF was figuring out how to make agents work, for example the Autogen orchestration framework and the Fara computer use agent. In NYC however, several of us were interested in developing new fundamental capabilities such as the Next Latent objective which enables extrapolation, Dion3 which creates an optimized/improved Muon, or the Full Bandwidth Transformer which efficiently makes models function substantially more powerfully via recursion.

We also actively tried to share with the rest of MSR. For example, AIF decided to develop a monorepo that was shared by default with all of Microsoft Research. In this monorepo for example was the proven-capable edge scale pretraining codebase I talked about in the COLM keynote last month. This might seem like a minor detail, but the amount effort required to create a well-formed model creation pipeline is substantial and I’m aware of at least 4 efforts (the other 3 not in public-within-MSR repos) trying to develop model building pipelines.

In early September we were reorged into Microsoft AI . On the surface this could make sense, because putting two different AI organizations together creates opportunities for better concentration of effort, and there were places where AIF was ahead of MAI and of course vice-versa (MAI is much larger). In practice, there are substantial issues because the philosophy of the ex- Inflection leadership of MAI is incompatible. The core philosophy there is scaling, and aggressively not research. This might shock some folks who naturally think that the way you make better models is via research but there is plenty of evidence that bigger models are better models as far as the quality of the predictions they make and from a business perspective returns to scale are far more predictable than returns to research. In a scaling-only environment of course the primary effort is on getting/making/refining data, which is quite a step away from what we were working on. Aside from the incompatible focus, there was plenty of evidence that they just did not really want us.

It’s a tough situation to find yourself in. I consider the scaling-only focus to be both misdirected and not fun. It is an understandable failure mode—scaling is straightforward and it’s common for people to give up on a tradeoff between multiple competing ideals (like innovation and size) by short-sightedly adopting one in totality and dropping the other. But returns to research are real and significant. For example, the Bytedance experiments suggest a variant of the Full Bandwidth Transformer might be comparable to a model of twice the size, implying significant savings in training and inference for the same capability. Do the math—how much is it worth to halve training and inference cost given that the industry has investments…

items.title: Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers
items.summary: release
items.content:
Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers

Contents Nspawn 3.0: A Docker-compatible Engine API for systemd-nspawn containers

2.0.0 gave the machines that mount docker’s socket a read-only Docker API, enough for Traefik or Dozzle to find them. 3.0.0 serves the API with its changes, on the host too. In between:

2.1.0: published ports answer over IPv6 too, and -p takes IPv6 addresses. 2.2.0: fixes for what came up moving a whole server of compose projects to nspawn. compose got anonymous volumes, networks made again when their definition changes, down SERVICE and a start that brings up what a service depends on. 2.3.0: every layer is applied inside the tree it is extracted into and checked against the digest its image names for it. 2.3.1: packages on apt.nspawn.org (Debian 13+, Ubuntu 24.04+) and rpm.nspawn.org (Fedora 44+). 2.4.0: -p PORT takes a free port of the host, and a pull of an image index picks the entry for the host’s platform. The Docker Engine API on the host

The host’s socket is /run/nspawn/api.sock , opened by nspawn-api.socket . Its main purpose is compatibility: tools that manage containers through the Docker API, like GitLab Runner’s docker executor, can use nspawn’s machines instead. nspawn is still the command line for managing them, but the docker command works against the socket too.

The packages ship the socket turned off. Once it listens, nspawn-api.service starts on the first connection:

$ sudo systemctl enable --now nspawn-api.socket

With DOCKER_HOST pointing at it, the docker command talks to nspawn:

$ export DOCKER_HOST = unix:///run/nspawn/api.sock

$ docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx

The API server is a client of the bus service, as the command line is. Everything it does is a method of org.nspawn , under the same polkit actions: reads and waits need org.nspawn.inspect , logs and changes need org.nspawn.manage . Every user can connect, but polkit is never asked to prompt, since nothing on a socket can answer an authentication agent. Root can do everything, and any other user needs a polkit rule, like nspawn-wheel.rules , which the packages ship as an example. As with the docker group, a user with org.nspawn.manage is root on the host: a machine runs commands as root and can mount any host path.

What one socket’s clients hold at once (connections, log and event streams, waits, attaches, execs) is bounded, and a user other than root gets a share of each, so no user can keep the others or root out.

Clients that only look at /run/docker.sock find it with a drop-in, on a host where nothing else has that path:

$ sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/nspawn-api.socket.d

$ printf '[Socket]\nSymlinks=/run/docker.sock\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/nspawn-api.socket.d/symlink.conf

$ sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart nspawn-api.socket

It answers in the shapes of API 1.51, and of the versions down to 1.24 that clients ask for.

Containers: create , start , stop , restart , kill , pause , unpause , wait , update , remove and prune, with AutoRemove . A create’s settings become the machine’s options: what nspawn has no use for comes back in Warnings , and what would change what the container does is refused with 400. attach: with the input too. The program gets the client’s input, and its output comes back byte for byte, which is what docker run -i , docker run -it and docker start -ai use. exec: with a terminal or with stdout and stderr apart, input, variables, working directory and user. A command that is not found exits 127, one that can’t run 126. archive: HEAD , GET and PUT on /containers/ID/archive , so docker cp works both ways, on running and stopped containers, keeping owners and modes. Images: pull, with the engine’s progress messages and its “Image is up to date” and “Downloaded newer image”, remove and prune. An image’s ID is its config’s digest. Volumes and networks: create, inspect, list, remove and prune, and connect and…

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: Remember When Bosses Were Forcing Their Workers to Use AI? They’re Now Realizing They Made a Huge Mistake: "AI is changing not only how we work, but also how we judge the people we work with."
items.content:
For years, many bosses have been adamant that employees use AI at all costs — despite research suggesting there’s little to gain from it in terms of productivity , evidence that flies in the face of the tech industry’s repeated promises of a workplace revolution brought on by the tech.

But now that execs are drowning in meaningless “ workslop ,” they’re starting to sing a very different tune. As Business Insider reports , one CEO of a tech recruiting company suddenly found herself being inundated with Slack messages from employees that they’d clearly generated using AI, leading her to implement a new policy that strictly forbids the practice for internal communications.

She’s not the first. One anonymous CEO got so fed up, they threatened to “fire the next person ” who blasted them with unedited ChatGPT slop, as Inc reported earlier this year . Instead of fundamentally reshaping white collar industries for the better, it’s finally dawning on bosses that the extensive and often counterproductive use of AI tools could be doing far more harm than good.

Case in point, in a new study published in the journal The Leadership Quarterly , a team of researchers led by Hebrew University of Jerusalem PhD student Samuel Meyers found that employees who doubled down on using tools like ChatGPT are being trusted less by their employers, actively hurting their chances of promotion.

That’s even at workplaces where the use of AI tools are still actively being encouraged, suggesting there’s a paradoxical price workers who embrace the tech are paying.

In a series of experiments, the team asked supervisors to decide whether to trust an employee’s report, while knowing whether they had used AI or not — but not basing their judgment on the quality of the work itself. Employees who didn’t use AI had a 68 percent chance of earning their trust. When they used AI, that number shrank down to just 24 percent.

“AI is changing not only how we work, but also how we judge the people we work with,” said coauthor and Hebrew University of Jerusalem senior lecturer Yochanan Bigman in a statement . “An employee may use AI to produce better work more efficiently yet still lose their manager’s trust simply because AI was involved.”

As a result, “organizations need to recognize that adopting AI is not just a technological challenge — it is also a psychological and managerial one,” Bigman added.

Beyond eroding trust, executives have also found that the use of AI agents and coding tools in particular have sent costs soaring, seriously hurting their companies’ bottom lines and often forcing them to reverse course and cut spending .

Meanwhile, researchers have yet to detect a meaningful windfall from using AI at work, making it an expensive distraction. Polls have shown that the vast majority of CEOs haven’t seen any productivity gains.

It’s a particularly unfortunate reality as the job market continues to deteriorate , with or without any AI-related productivity boost.

Employees are now stuck between a rock in a hard place: either follow their supervisors’ instructions and use AI, or earn their trust by ignoring those calls. Meyers and his colleagues worry this growing tension could give rise to “shadow AI” — undisclosed use of the tech at work, that could further hurt their career prospects.

items.title: 글 쌌다 지웠다 하는 뷩쉰은 봐라
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…
