items.title: sshole: OpenSSH on musl without PAM lets * accounts in with any 256+ byte password (fixed 5 Nov)
items.content:
Quick summary · TL;DR **The accounts at risk are the ones with * in the password field.** Key-only users and the tiny-cloud alpine user have it, and when sshd runs on musl without PAM they accept any password over 256 bytes once another account has a real hash. Root has it too, but the default PermitRootLogin keeps it off password logins.

On Alpine, compare the package release, not the version string. Stable branches got backports, so a patched 3.24 box reports 10.3_p1-r2, and only edge carries 10.6_p2-r0.

Restart sshd after the upgrade. Alpine's advisory says apk upgrade alone leaves the vulnerable daemon running, which is easy to miss on a box nobody logs into.

PasswordAuthentication no is the quick workaround. Test a key login in a second session before the restart, since getting it wrong can lock you out of a remote box.

The sshole OpenSSH vulnerability lets an account whose password field is just * log in with any password longer than 256 bytes. It hits Alpine and anything else built on musl libc where sshd checks passwords without PAM, as long as one other account has a real hash. Fixing it takes OpenSSH 10.6p2 or your distro’s patched package, plus an sshd restart.

That * is the nasty part, because key-only users, directory users and root on Alpine since about 3.16 all carry it. Root is saved by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password , unless another reachable account can doas to it.

What the sshole OpenSSH vulnerability is

Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield reported it, and OpenSSH shipped 10.6p2 on 2026-11-05 . Its release notes call it “a critical security workaround” for musl systems with PAM disabled and place the root cause outside sshd.

MITRE published CVE-2026-123158 the same day, scored 8.1 (CVSS 3.1, attack complexity high). Alpine’s advisory of 2026-11-05 says no CVE had been assigned yet.

You’re exposed only when all five hold. That’s the researcher’s list, and Alpine’s advisory carries the last four:

sshd runs on musl (Alpine, and per sshhole.com also OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto)

sshd does not use PAM (Alpine’s openssh-server is built without it, and openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no counts too)

PasswordAuthentication yes , which is the OpenSSH default

some account has exactly * as its password field

at least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ hash

cloud-init images (they write PasswordAuthentication no )

Glibc distros, Dropbear and OpenBSD are safe too, per the researcher.

In August 2012 musl changed crypt() to return an unmatchable hash instead of NULL on failure, which is * in this case. Weeks later its SHA-256 and SHA-512 crypt set a 256-byte key limit, so a longer password fails and gets that * back. And since a 2016 timing fix for CVE-2016-6210, sshd hashes the attempt with another account’s salt when the stored field has none.

So sshd compares * with * , and the login goes through. OpenSSH’s upstream fix refuses any stored field shorter than four characters.

For the sshole OpenSSH vulnerability, stable branches carry a backported patch under the old version number, so sshd -V on a patched 3.24 box still says 10.3, not 10.6p2. Compare the package release instead (Alpine advisory and package index, 2026-11-06):

Run apk upgrade -U -a , then rc-service sshd restart , since upgrading leaves the old daemon running.

OpenWrt’s default SSH server is Dropbear, per its wiki . If you swapped in the openssh-server package, the packages feed took fixes on 2026-11-05: 10.6p2 on master and openwrt-25.12 (10.6_p2-r1), and a backport on openwrt-24.10 that ships as 9.9_p2-r2, the same version trap as on Alpine. On 2026-11-06 mipsel_24kc on 24.10 still served 9.9_p2-r1, so check your router’s build.

sshd -T | grep -E '^(usepam|passwordauthentication) '

items.title: Asahi Linux Progress Linux 7.3
items.content:
Well here we are again. Linux 7.3 is out and it’s been an eventful few months, so

let’s get stuck in to another Asahi Linux progress report!

As always, upstreaming work continues to progress. Aside from the usual patches for

low-level SoC blocks, two major drivers made it on to the list this cycle: macaudio

and avd. Getting macaudio ready for submission has been a challenge. The audio subsystem

on Apple Silicon devices is rather special, and required quite a number of core ALSA

changes to properly support it. Apple also uses special variants of speaker and headset

amplifiers that were already supported upstream, and these drivers also needed some

pretty significant modifications. We have previously discussed a lot of this work at

length, and we are finally in a position where we can submit the main driver for

review. The driver and Devicetree changes represent a hefty chunk of our total patchset,

AVD is a whole different beast. The AVD driver has spent barely 3 months in our downstream

tree and is already on the list. This is our shortest turnaround time yet for a major

SoC component and bodes well for a transition to upstream-first development some time

in the future. This is fantastic news, as the AVD driver and related Devicetree changes

Also making an appearance on the list this cycle are initial Devicetrees not only for M4 Pro

and Max devices but also M5 thanks to Yureka’s tireless efforts. As usual these initial

Devicetrees are barebones and only sufficient to boot the SoC to a TTY, however work

is progressing on further enablement. Watch this space!

We have also begun shifting to an upstream-first approach where practical. Changes

to the TI USB-PD and SPMI drivers required for new devices, as well as initial support

for Thunderbolt, were all developed upstream-first. We are so thrilled to see

our focus on upstreaming starting to pay off!

Last time, we announced initial support for M3 series machines via the EXPERT flag on

the Asahi installer. We are pleased to announce that we received almost no issues

from early adopters, so M3 support is now generally available without the EXPERT flag!

We have also made a number of improvements to M3 support, most notably enabling DCP.

On top of performance and battery life improvements, this also allows us to enable

sleep on M3 series devices and make the area around the notch useable on the MacBooks!

Keep an eye out for m1n1 and kernel updates in the coming days.

Last time, we teased support for virtualising SPTM-enabled versions of macOS in m1n1,

which enables reverse engineering on M4 series machines. M5 presents a new challenge,

as the versions of macOS which support it all require the use of Exclaves.

Exclaves are small applications running in an isolated environment controlled by the

Secure Kernel. On M5 series SoCs and above, macOS uses them for sensitive tasks

such as drawing the “camera in use” indicator to the screen. XNU communicates with

the Secure Kernel and its Exclaves via SPTM, using yet another IPC protocol called

Tightbeam. Much as with SPTM, XNU will panic if it cannot find the running Exclaves.

This is all starting to look very similar in concept to Arm’s own TrustZone feature.

While some Exclaves can be bypassed by changing some settings on the command line,

we predict that this will not always be the case. As such, Sven started looking at how we

could fit all of this in to m1n1. First line of investigation, try putting the

Secure Kernel and Exclave userspace in another VM next to SPTM and macOS.

and we’re now up to spawning three VMs in EL1 under m1n1! Maybe we can start

selling m1n1 to companies fleeing VMWare… With that, we can now virtualise

and reverse engineer macOS on both M4 and M5 series machines.

While M3 support is now mostly at feature parity with M1 and M2, the very obvious exception

to this is the GPU. Apple’s GPU team seems to follow a tick-tock model, and the M3’s

items.title: *sshole, or when are we finally going to get rid of C?
items.summary: rant
items.content:
Yet another day, yet another vulnerability in core C code. This one happened due to two different conditions using the same sentinel value:

The two points combined, along with sshd hashing login attempts for locked accounts to avoid timing leaks, mean that on musl systems without PAM (like, oh, the official Alpine AWS image ), an unauthenticated user now gets a (possibly root!) shell on your computer. See this Alpine advisory for more details.

This is not a memory safety vulnerability; rather, it is one of those issues that, people often say, languages with better type systems won’t save you from. This is true! You can very well write a Rust function that returns "*" if the password is too long. But the big difference between C and Rust in this regard is that the norms of the Rust community do not allow that .

The POSIX spec tries to account for error cases. It says :

Upon successful completion, crypt() shall return a pointer to the hashed password; […] Otherwise, it shall return a null pointer and set errno to indicate the error.

But the C type system can’t force developers to check that the return value is NULL. The musl libc developers saw that some binaries weren’t checking for it, and as a result deviated from the spec, returning the sentinel "*" value instead.

As I’ve written about before , type systems have a strong effect on engineering culture. Because C doesn’t have algebraic data types or result types, the engineering norms that form around C communities lead to this kind of in-band signaling. Meanwhile, in Rust, a password that’s too long would be returned as an error variant, and the caller would be compelled to handle it. What if there isn’t an error variant today? Then a breaking change would add an error variant, and a RustSec advisory would probably be published as well.

As an aside, it remains surprising to me when Linux distro maintainers complain about projects introducing Rust dependencies. Rather than adapting to the new world where the engineering norms are likely to serve users better, these maintainers insist on the world adapting to them. Yes, compile times and portability to niche architectures are real costs, but are you here to serve your own interests or the bulk of your users’? There’s a real principal-agent problem going on here.

Speaking of agents! There’s a recent strain of argument that goes roughly like this:

There is plenty that’s wrong about the argument, including the dubious decision to trust a fuzzy process when we have already shown that a far more deterministic approach works. But the big missing piece is the norms of the respective communities! When you (or your agent) write Rust software, you’re probably going to use Rust libraries, and your agent is probably going to pattern-match on existing Rust code in its training set. As a result, even if you aren’t already a skilled Rust developer , there will likely be more invariants encoded in the type system 1 .

The engineering norms of C developers allow for "*" to be an acceptable sentinel value indicating an error; the engineering norms of Rust developers simply do not. These norms are the result of the accumulated contributions of a community, and part of the responsibility of a software professional is to think about the kinds of communities one’s work is a part of. But some people have decided that none of this really matters in this shiny new world, and that the contributions of other people can mostly be ignored. Their hubris will be their downfall.

If you’re a skilled Rust developer, you’ll likely find the first-pass invariants the agent encodes to be woefully inadequate, and you’ll probably go through a long review cycle where those kinds of issues are fixed.  ↩︎
items.title_ko: *sshole, 우리는 언제쯤 C를 버릴 수 있을까?
items.summary_ko: 두 조건이 같은 센티넬 값("*")을 사용하면서 sshd에 취약점이 생겼다. musl 기반 시스템에서 PAM 없이 동작하는 경우(예: 공식 Alpine AWS 이미지) 인증되지 않은 사용자가 루트일 수도 있는 셸을 얻을 수 있다. 메모리 안전성 문제는 아니며, C의 타입 시스템이 반환값 검사를 강제하지 못하는 점이 원인으로 지적된다.
items.content_ko: 또 하나의 핵심 C 코드 취약점이다. 두 가지 조건이 같은 센티넬 값을 사용했고, 여기에 잠긴 계정의 로그인 시도를 타이밍 누출을 막기 위해 해시 처리하는 sshd의 동작이 겹쳤다. 그 결과 musl 기반 시스템에서 PAM을 쓰지 않는 경우(예: 공식 Alpine AWS 이미지) 인증되지 않은 사용자가 (루트일 수도 있는) 셸을 얻게 된다. 글쓴이는 이것이 메모리 안전성 문제가 아니며, 더 나은 타입 시스템을 가진 언어가 있다고 해서 자동으로 막을 수 있는 문제도 아니라고 설명한다. Rust에서도 비밀번호가 너무 길면 "*"를 반환하는 함수를 작성할 수 있지만, Rust 커뮤니티의 관행상 그런 코드는 허용되지 않는다는 점이 차이라고 말한다. POSIX 명세는 crypt()가 오류 시 NULL 포인터를 반환하고 errno를 설정한다고 규정하지만, C 타입 시스템은 개발자가 NULL 반환값을 확인하도록 강제할 수 없다. musl 개발자들은 일부 바이너리가 이 반환값을 확인하지 않는 것을 발견했다. (원문이 중간에 끊겨 있다.)

items.title: Goodbye Claude, Hello Pi
items.content:
I’ve been a longtime Claude Code user, ever since it became available in the Claude Pro subscription plan over a year ago. I remember the first time I used it, feeling giddy as it spat out messy Python code for whatever random weekend project I was working on, all from a single prompt. I’m certain that in a few years we’ll all look back at its release as one of the major drivers of this new era of software development we’re in.

Despite this, due to an accumulation of many small frustrations, I’ve finally decided to retire it as my main coding harness and migrate my development setup to use Pi instead.

Someone at Anthropic must’ve caught wind… just a day after making my decision, they announced Claude Code would finally start supporting AGENTS.md files in an effort to get me to stay. Unfortunately, for me it was too little, too late.

In lieu of a proper obituary, I’d like to take this time to say a few words about the things I liked least about Claude Code (and thus what I’m looking forward to avoiding with Pi).

The AGENTS.md thing kind of epitomizes the whole reason I decided to quit using Claude Code. Don’t get me wrong, having a ton of CLAUDE.md files scattered about various GitHub hobby repos is great guerrilla marketing. But it sucks for users to have to deal with copying or symlinking between the two formats.

Like the Luddite I am, I still prefer to review most of the code it churns out before I commit it. I use(d) Claude Code inside VSCode, and it lets you connect the harness to the IDE. This is nice because you can highlight text in a file and have it automatically included in the context when asking questions or requesting changes during a review.

Except you can only have one session “connected” to the IDE at a time. If you open a second tab to start another task while the first one works, it can’t receive the text selection events from the IDE at all. This has been reported at least as far back as December 2025 … and closed as a duplicate of a totally unrelated bug. 1

Of course, you can always use the official Claude Code VSCode GUI extension, which does allow you to have multiple tabs open and load the text selection into the context of each. But this extension has plenty of problems of its own. Half of the built-in slash commands don’t work at all in the GUI. It doesn’t have any support for a custom status line. Subagent output messages are simply layered into the main chat thread in chronological order, which is a mess to read when more than one is running. I could go on and on.

In spite of all of these existing issues, it seems like Anthropic has worked at a feverish pace to pack more features into Claude Code without much care for quality or stability. Dynamic workflows , agent teams , ultrareviews – all great ways to help enterprise customers burn ever more tokens each day, but not really anything I want or need.

Alongside all of these feature releases, they always seem to be fiddling with things in ways that mess up my personal setup. At the time of writing, there have been 244 releases to Claude Code this year; over 3/4 of these changed the system prompt or tool descriptions, which can substantially change how the LLM performs (especially when these new instructions contradict user prompts or repo conventions).

And what are all those changes for? Despite chopping 80% of the system prompt , Claude Code still has way more overhead than Pi for seemingly no benefit. The default Bash tool’s description is almost 3,000 tokens, most of which is random stuff about using git and opening PRs on GitHub. 2 The models already know how to do this without detailed instructions, by the way. 3

This post has been a lot of hating. I’m sorry! That’s not my usual style, and I do think Anthropic has made a really cool piece of software here. I’m also not under any delusion that I would’ve done a better job if I were the one in charge of running Claude Code from the beginning. LLM coding harnesses are a very new space…

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Hands on with the AYN Odin 3 Portal; All You Need, and Then Some
items.content:
I've been writing about so-called retro handhelds for a long time now, but I'm beginning to wonder whether the term has lost almost all meaning. It made perfect sense when we were primarily talking about little Linux-powered devices designed to play Game Boy, SNES and PlayStation games. These days, however, we're looking at Android handhelds capable of tackling Nintendo Switch games, increasingly demanding PC titles, PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 emulation, even Switch 2 games these last few weeks. We've moved so far beyond what most people would reasonably consider retro gaming that I suspect we're going to need a new name for these things sooner or later. And nothing illustrates that better than the AYN Odin 3 Portal.

What's remarkable about the Odin 3 Portal isn't necessarily the approach AYN has taken, because we've seen it before. The original Odin 2 Portal followed much the same formula, taking the already powerful Odin 2 and giving it a larger display, design and some welcome refinements, while retaining essentially the same performance. What's particularly impressive this time is that the original Odin 3 arrived in late 2025, bringing Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite-class Dragonwing Q8 processor to the handheld market, and roughly a year later, that same hardware remains among the most powerful available in an Android handheld. AYN hasn't needed to chase another generational leap in performance to make the Odin 3 Portal compelling. Instead, it's doing what the Portal range was always intended to do, taking an already extraordinarily capable machine and offering it in a larger, arguably more luxurious format. It's an interesting position for a manufacturer to find itself in, especially in a market where new devices seem to appear almost weekly, promising ever greater performance.

Of course, that doesn't mean the Portal is simply an Odin 3 with a bigger screen. The six-inch display has grown to a lovely seven-inch, 120Hz OLED panel, the battery has increased from 8,000mAh to 9,000mAh, and AYN has made some welcome changes to the controls and ergonomics. Full-sized analogue sticks, a more substantial body and quieter face buttons address some of the practical concerns that have accompanied earlier handhelds, where even something as seemingly insignificant as the sound of a button press could become an irritation. These might not be the sort of changes that make headlines alongside a new processor, but they're precisely the things that can make a handheld considerably more enjoyable to actually use.

Technology for Human Beings. We tell human stories at the intersection of tech and culture. Free software, gaming, movies, music, TV, and the industries that have colonized our lives.

AYN has also managed to retain what I think is one of its greatest strengths: offering something that feels super premium without demanding the sort of money we've increasingly come to associate with high-end handheld gaming. With memory and storage prices causing no end of trouble for manufacturers, and several companies already having to increase prices or reconsider hardware configurations, the Odin 3 Portal's introductory starting price of $399 isn’t unreasonable. AYN itself has been forced to increase prices on the original Odin 3 several times throughout 2026, which makes the Portal's pricing all the more impressive. Granted, that entry-level ‘Base’ model only includes 128GB of storage, which won't go particularly far once you start exploring more demanding emulation, but there's still an awful lot of hardware here for the money. AYN has long occupied the more luxurious end of the Android handheld market, but there's a certain restraint to its approach this time. Rather than introducing another generation of processor, the company has concentrated on refining an already excellent foundation.

items.title: Every Windows 11 app should kill Electron, and Discord just showed why
items.content:
Discord’s current Electron client and its new Rust client launching side by side on two Lenovo ThinkPads running Windows 11

Discord’s new Rust client had its friends list loaded before the current Electron app could get past its loading screen, in a 15-second clip that we found on the X account of Discord co-founder and CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy . The video had 2.3 million views at the time of writing, and Discord employees have confirmed that both apps were launched from a cold start.

Vishnevskiy also revealed that the 290.2MB RAM usage on the Task Manager of the new client, which shows up as Discord Phoenix, came with two accounts signed in at once, which justifies the already efficient RAM usage.

Discord’s Rust client opens before the Electron app finishes loading

“The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time,” Vishnevskiy wrote on X , and Discord’s official account also shared the clip with the current client on the left and the Rust rebuild on the right.

https://www.windowslatest.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Electron-Discord-vs-Rust-Discord-where-the-new-client-opens-must-faster-than-the-old-one.mp4

We went through the video frame by frame. What’s impressive is that the current client is opened first and shows a blank dark window for about three seconds, followed by a tip that reads “In the ancient days, Discord started as a browser-only app.” Funnily enough, the Electron app still carries a browser engine today.

The new client is double-clicked roughly a second and a half later, yet its window fades in within a second. When the old app reaches its interface, about five seconds after launch, the Rust version already has the friends list loaded, while the Electron client briefly says “There are no friends online at this time.”

Discord Windows app. Credit: Windows Latest

Of course, people on X asked if the new app simply popped out of the system tray. “Both are cold starts, it’s really that fast. We’ve been using it internally now for a while and the first time I tried it I thought I’d forgot to close it when I opened it fresh,” replied Coral, who leads audio and video at Discord.

Travis, who works on socials and community at Discord and filmed the clip, added that a tray launch would mean “the friends list would have already been loaded!” Vishnevskiy thanked him for “finding these janky old laptops,” which are ThinkPads with a Copilot key, so 2024 or newer, which I wouldn’t dare call janky or old. They’re beautiful machines!

The new Discord app skips the “Starting” screen and updates in the background

As you’d already know, the current app usually checks for updates and shows a “Starting” screen when you open it, which one person on X said “takes like 5-10s every time.” Asked why the new client skips it, coral said, “It bootstraps so fast + is a new architecture so we don’t need that modal at all. We auto-update in the background.”

Discord starting animation. Credit: Windows Latest

Discord isn’t handing updates to the Microsoft Store or Windows’ Update Orchestration Platform either, as Coral said “We do not at this moment” when asked.

Discord’s Rust client uses about 70% less RAM with two accounts signed in

When one reply called 290MB “still vile” for a chat app, Vishnevskiy said, “Those 4k avatar decorations gotta render somewhere ;) but joking aside this client is actually running 2 accounts concurrently which is supported in new client.”

Today’s Account Switcher lets you add up to five accounts and swap between them. Asked if the new client could keep work and personal accounts running “without needing to tear down the client in between,” Vishnevskiy replied “Yup.” Again, impressive and exciting.

Discord idle RAM usage. Credit: Windows Latest

For comparison, a Discord employee said in December 2025 that normal usage is under 1GB, while the company tested auto-restarting the app at 4GB . So, 290.2MB is about…

Update 5: Instagram is now leaking recovery email and phone numbers linked to an account.

Seems like every day a new security issue crops up at Instagram.

According to the claim, when a newly created account is routed through a Los Angeles-based VPN and then submits a specific mix of reports in scam and fraud category, the targeted account can allegedly be banned without any human review.

Instagram Account Banning by AI by Reporting Scam and Fraud (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 3: Meta’s apparent fix for the AI bot vulnerability is difficult to take seriously. Instead of fully disabling the risky functionality, they reportedly removed it from the visible interface while leaving the underlying API endpoint accessible. Hiding the button may stop regular users from seeing the feature, but it does nothing if attackers can still reach the same workflow directly through the API.

Meta Hid AI Chatbot from UI (Source: X/Twitter)

Update 2: Yet another Instagram account-takeover trick is reportedly being abused, this time involving Meta’s AI chatbot. Sellers are allegedly using modified Instagram builds on Android emulators like BlueStacks, then manipulating the AI with hidden characters and carefully worded prompts to force username changes. The method is reportedly being used to grab rare OG handles, including one-letter usernames, and handle-monitoring bots have already flagged several suspicious swaps.

New Instagram AI Exploit (Source: X/Twitter)

A natural language interface sitting in front of account-level APIs. No hard authentication gate before executing state changes. items.title: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam
items.content:
Activists scale a temporary construction fence at the site of a new Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam. Photograph: Michel Van Bergen/AP

Activists scale a temporary construction fence at the site of a new Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam. Photograph: Michel Van Bergen/AP

Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam

Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom

Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.

Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort, Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.

The action comes amid Europe-wide resistance to the rapid expansion of energy-hungry AI, with more than 100 groups involved in a two-day series of protests to demand moratoria on the construction of new datacentres.

Geef Tegengas activists attach a ‘Genocide’ banner to scaffolding at the Microsoft site. Photograph: Storm Groenendijk/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock The break-in at the Dutch site, where protesters hung banners objecting to Microsoft’s services to the Israeli military and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) , was separate from the pan-European “Stop Dirty Data Centres” campaign, which targeted the same site but whose affiliated members stayed outside the perimeter fence.

Police said in a statement to NOS, a Dutch public broadcaster: “The police attempted to prevent [the occupation] and arrest protesters, but were unable to prevent it and force was used.

“An officer was slightly injured during the protest.”

Protesters from both groups said police used force and teargas to dispel the activists trying to enter the construction site. Organisers and local media reported hundreds of protesters on each side of the fence.

Smaller protests took place in the centre of Bristol, in the UK, at a datacentre in Berlin, Germany, outside the Polish parliament in Warsaw and at the main square in Zagreb, Croatia. Further protests are expected on Saturday.

Activists across Europe prepare two days of protests against datacentres

Stop Dirty Data Centres, a coalition of independent groups that include national branches of Greenpeace and Friends of the Earth, said it had not coordinated or promoted the direct action that took place in the Netherlands , but that is was “understandable” communities would turn to a range of tactics when they were unable to meaningfully participate in decision-making.

“Big tech and government are racing ahead with large-scale datacentre development despite significant public concern about the impacts on local communities, natural resources and other industries,” said Owen Espley, campaign coordinator. “Many datacentre developments are planned with limited transparency or scrutiny, while communities across Europe are being shut out of decisions that will shape their local environments and futures.”

Protesters sit on top of a wall at the Microsoft datacentre site. Photograph: Fadel Dawod/Getty Images The ecological fallout of the datacentre boom has alarmed some climate scientists, while growing frustration with AI’s societal impact – from energy bills and job losses to the role of tech companies in undermining democracy – has increased public anger. In the US midterm elections this week, nearly every proposed moratorium on datacentres on the ballot was approved.

Roos Molenaar, an activist from Geef Tegengas, said the struggle against big tech was inseparable from the fight against oppression and fascism. “We won’t accept Amsterdam being used for the creation of AI slop and the facilitation of genocide,” said Molenaar. “This datacentre is gulping up our drinking water to make the rich even richer.”

items.title: TUXEDO OS Enters Final Beta Testing Ahead of Debian-Based Release
items.content:
TUXEDO Computers has just announced that its upcoming Debian-based TUXEDO OS has entered the final stage of its open beta. That brings the Linux distro right up to the point of being fully transitioned away from Ubuntu.

The new edition, known as TUXEDO OS “Continuous Debian,” replaces the distribution’s traditional Ubuntu foundation with Debian Testing. The change denotes a significant shift for TUXEDO OS, which is developed by German Linux hardware manufacturer TUXEDO Computers.

Open beta testing started in August , and since then the dev team has issued five beta ISOs. The company has reported a large number of bug reports as a result of the testing, as well as a lot of positive feedback from users who have been running the new system without any issues.

TUXEDO OS Debian-based beta running KDE Plasma 6.7.4 on Wayland with Linux kernel 7.2.7.

As for the software, the current beta runs KDE Plasma 6.7.4 on Wayland, alongside KDE Frameworks 6.30 , Qt 6.11.2, and Linux kernel 7.2 . Unlike Debian itself, which periodically promotes its Testing branch to Stable, TUXEDO OS will remain permanently based on Debian Testing.

TUXEDO Computers will also continue maintaining its own package repositories and providing updates for key components, including the kernel, graphics drivers, and KDE Plasma.

Throughout November, the development team is concentrating on handling outstanding bug reports and handling remaining issues before the first stable release. Users participating in the testing program are encouraged to report not previously identified bugs or unanticipated behavior as soon as possible.

However, bug fixing is not the only thing left to do. TUXEDO Computers also needs to establish and validate a suite of structured, automated QA test procedures. Those tests have to be run before they can actually set a release date.

As for when the stable Debian-based TUXEDO OS will be arriving, the developers have not given us a date at this point. They do, however, expect to be able to release it fairly soon once the final testing and QA are complete.

For additional information, see the announcement .

Those interested in testing the upcoming Debian-based TUXEDO OS before its stable release can download the latest beta ISO images from the preview download directory .

items.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
items.content:
We changed requirements in a coding benchmark and found models talking themselves out of following them.

Sometimes the agent understood the new requirement perfectly. It described what needed to change, considered an implementation, and then decided the hidden tests probably wanted something else. In one run, a model implemented the change correctly, asked another model for the benchmark’s original answer, and removed its own correct code after receiving it.

This is an awkward habit for a coding assistant to have. It is also a habit that a familiar benchmark can reward. If the model has guessed what the tests expect, it gets the same passing result as an agent that worked carefully from the requirements.

We built MaxxBench to examine how much coding performance depends on those expectations. It changes the instructions or starting code of 89 DeepSWE tasks, giving models familiar engineering work with a reason to revise their usual approach.

Once a benchmark becomes popular, it becomes part of the development process. Its tasks can enter training data. Its scores influence checkpoint selection. Developers adjust prompts and agents against its failures. There are plenty of opportunities to get better at that particular exam. We call gains tied to its particular tasks and conventions benchmaxxing .

Then the scores cluster near the top, and the usual response is a harder benchmark. Recent releases such as FrontierSWE v2 have pushed toward engineering projects that can occupy an agent for much of a day.

We chose DeepSWE’s medium-duration feature-implementation tasks because they are closer to the everyday coding work we wanted to evaluate. Before adding more work, we wanted to know how well models would handle changes to the tasks they already scored well on.

For example, one DeepSWE task asks an agent to write a separate test report for each browser. We added a requirement that the filenames be lowercase. The reporting feature still needs to work; Chrome.xml should now be chrome.xml .

Another task adds retirement dates to FastAPI routes. We changed the required timestamps to UTC with a trailing Z , instead of preserving the supplied time-zone offset.

Each browser writes its own report file, replacing spaces and punctuation with underscores;

MaxxBench also requires lowercase filenames.

Browser name Example browser names Chrome Chrome (Headless) firefox

reports/ C h r o m e _ _ H e a d l e s s _ . x m l

reports/ c h r o m e _ _ h e a d l e s s _ . x m l

These changes resemble requests a developer might make after reviewing a first implementation. The agent has to keep the feature working while adjusting its behavior.

Other mutations change the code around the feature, including the interfaces available to implement it. We revise the reference solution and tests accordingly, retaining checks for behavior that still applies. That gives us two related versions of the work and a way to inspect where an agent’s adaptation succeeds or fails.

Across all tasks, MaxxBench’s reference patches grow by a median of just 17 lines (3.5%). Handling menial revisions of this size should be routine for a capable coding agent.

Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 3.8 Flash both have published DeepSWE scores of about 74%. On MaxxBench, they score 76.4% and 53.4%.

A 23-point gap is a different basis for choosing between them. The original scores make them look like peers; the revised tasks expose a large difference in how reliably they handle changes to the work.

GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5 also start close together on DeepSWE, then separate to 71.9% and 63.5% on MaxxBench.

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: It Turns Out Binance's $6 Billion Hack Happened Because Its Employees Were Vibe Coding
items.content:
Billions of dollars of crypto stolen — in a hack that we’re now learning involved corporate vibe coding efforts. You couldn’t come up with a more quintessential cautionary tale for an era when employers are embracing AI at every level.

After hackers drained nearly $6.3 billion from the crypto platform , Binance has revealed how the thieves pulled off what might be the heist of the century.

In a detailed report on its investigation published Tuesday, the company described an elaborate scheme that took place over months involving sham job interviews, old-fashioned phishing, and — yes — a hijacked AI tool.

It began in June when an employee on Binance’s wallet developer team thought they’d indulge in some vibe coding by installing a popular AI coding tool. But they ended up downloading a tampered installation of Homebrew, a tool that’s popular with software engineers, after clicking a malicious ad. Binance said it detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and changed relevant credentials.

So far so good, except that the attack exposed the role of the employee and his colleagues on the wallet team to the hackers, giving them the opening they needed. From there, some classic social engineering went into play. A hacker, posing as a project director, reached out to another software engineer through a legitimate job-hunting platform to offer an interview first with an “HR representative” and then the “CEO” of a fake company.

The fraudsters then earned the employee’s trust by sharing a social media account with personal photos and videos, something that Binance said “was more advanced and deceptive than previously seen social engineering approaches.” (It’s unclear from the report, but perhaps these were fabricated with AI, adding another element of AI menace to this story.)

Crucially, the follow-up interview was conducted over text. The engineer was asked to complete and download an “assignment” that contained malicious code that instantly executed once the employee began installing it. Among the things it changed was replacing a real development tool with a malicious version that could communicate with the hackers and execute commands.

That all took place in September. Starting in October, the hacker used the compromised employee machine to leverage an internal AI tool and use it as a “springboard” to seize control of the computer and the computer of a third wallet developer. From there, they used credentials stolen from the first wallet team employee to log into the third employee’s computer and trigger a malicious script that launched the attack.

In all, the attack siphoned 233.46 million XRP, a form of crypto, from five wallets into the hacker’s wallets, and then plundered other forms of crypto including bitcoin, in what may well have been the most lucrative heist of all time.

The culprits remain unclear. The FBI immediately blamed a notorious North Korean hacking outfit, but Pyongyang has denied involvement. Binance, in its report, noted that it had thwarted “57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases” — up until the big one that breached their defenses, at least.

items.title: GhostMap: The Android flaw that crashes your phone before you open the app
items.content:
Bitdefender Labs researchers found that installing a specially crafted app can leave an Android phone stuck in a crash loop, even if you never open it or grant it a single permission. The app contains no code and never needs to run.

After installation, a core system process crashes, restarts, and crashes again, leaving the phone stuck in a boot loop. Restarting doesn't help, and neither does safe mode.

To get the phone working again, you need a factory reset, which erases the user's data. If, by chance, USB debugging had already been enabled, you could use a computer with ADB (Android Debug Bridge) to delete the file before the phone reboots.

We began investigating on Aug. 12, 2026, when an APK collected from the wild crashed emulators in our analysis infrastructure. The sample was a banking dropper that never ran and crashed during installation.

When we looked closer to find out why, we found the problem wasn't the malware—it was the Android itself. The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file.

We call it GhostMap : the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.

Based on our testing, we consider the risk posed by this bug to be significant. In theory, an attacker could hide this technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of a factory reset and data loss as leverage for extortion. Malformed APKs could also disrupt tools that inspect Android applications. We have not observed any of these scenarios in the wild.

The banking dropper was wrapped by a packer. This is a tool that rewrites an APK's internal structure so reverse-engineering tools can't read it. It’s very common in modern Android malware.

In this case, the same rewrite also broke the Android component that parses an app during installation. That’s why the installation crashed in the first place and why our emulators failed on it. The good news is that nothing in the sample suggests the author knew the file would crash anything.

The sample did no more than that—a failed install. The underlying flaw runs deeper. We found that the same mistake can be aimed at a core system service instead of the installer, and there it produces the repeating crash loop described above, with no way back except a factory reset. That escalation is our own work; we have not seen it used against anyone.

The underlying problem concerns how Android trusts size and compression information in APK files, and it’s not limited to malformed ZIP files.

We reported the issue to Google twice through the Android & Devices Vulnerability Reward Program, expanding the second submission after further testing confirmed a persistent system crash loop.

items.title: 사생활침해 범죄가 의심 됩니다. 도움이 필요합니다
items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.

개별 이미지들의 위치 변경, 삭제, 별칭 추가, 폴더명 변경을 할 수 있습니다

items.content: 🚨 CVE-2026-114432 📢 Source: WPScan 💣 CVSS Score: 0.0 (NA) 📡 Remotely Exploitable: False The Contact Form 7 WordPress plugin before 6.2.4 does not validate the type or extension of files uploaded through a form file field, and a flaw in its temporary-file cleanup leaves the uploaded file on disk, allowing unauthenticated users to upload arbitrary files to the site. On a stock Debian or Ubuntu Apache configuration, which lists directory contents and maps .phar to the PHP handler, the stored file can be located and executed, leading to Remote Code Execution. On other configurations, including nginx and Apache with .htaccess overrides enabled, the issue is limited to an arbitrary file written into the uploads directory, which may still be served as active content such as HTML or SVG from the site's own origin. 📅 Published Date: 2026-11-08T06:00:29.249Z https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-114432
